changes.after: Use a default input or name the input you want to supply.

before: A named argument specifies the parameter it fills: bonus: 3 supplies the bonus parameter. Names make a call’s intent explicit.
A parameter declaration such as int bonus = 1 makes that parameter optional. Omitting its argument uses the declared default.
Passing bonus: 0 is not the same as leaving bonus out. Zero is a supplied value and replaces the default for this call.
The function body still operates on the parameter values. Optional and named arguments change how values are supplied, not how addition works.
Expected behavior from this example: 5 then 4. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Compare an omitted bonus, a zero bonus, and a positive bonus. Explain which value enters the function each time. You may trace it on paper if no C# toolchain is installed; reading completion does not certify a run.
after: A parameter is a named input in a function's definition. An argument is the value supplied when calling it. AddBonus has the parameters score and bonus.
The declaration int bonus = 1 gives bonus a default value. That makes the bonus argument optional.
If a call leaves out bonus, C# supplies 1. The score argument is still required because it has no default.
A named argument says which parameter receives a value. bonus: 0 sends zero to bonus. The colon connects the name with its value.
The program prints 5, then 4. The first call adds the default bonus of 1. The second call adds the supplied bonus of 0.
Leaving an argument out uses its default. Supplying zero uses zero. The function adds the values it receives either way.
